name: Photovoltaic Hemorrhage Emitter PHE-3 'Sunburn'
description: The PHE-3 operates by concentrating a narrow-band photovoltaic excitation beam tuned to the near-infrared absorption spectrum of hemoglobin and subcutaneous capillary tissue. On contact, the beam induces rapid localized vasodilation followed by catastrophic microvascular rupture beneath the skin's surface — a process that leaves no visible external wound for several seconds before hemorrhagic bruising blooms outward. The weapon draws on photonic resonance cycling technology developed by Arcturus Defense Solutions for orbital solar relay systems, miniaturized into a carbine-length chassis.
specifications:
length: 68 cm
weight: 3.1 kg
power source: Dual photovoltaic capacitor cell (ADS-PV9)
effective range: 8–120 m
beam wavelength: 780–850 nm NIR band
charge time: 1.4 seconds per pulse
shots per cell: 22 full-charge pulses
cooling system: Passive ceramic heat sink with gel-phase dissipation fins
tactical_use: Operators favor the PHE-3 for its delayed wound presentation — targets often continue moving for 4–8 seconds before systemic blood pressure drop incapacitates them, creating confusion among allied personnel. It is used in crowd infiltration scenarios where a clean, invisible first strike is needed before breaking contact. The weapon's lack of visible beam in standard lighting conditions and near-silent discharge make it effective for close-protection ambushes. Experienced operators layer pulses on a single target to accelerate hemorrhagic cascade rather than spreading fire.
cultural_context: The PHE-3 carries a deeply unsettling reputation in GLMZ's underground medical community — trauma surgeons at off-grid clinics have named the wound pattern 'sunburn syndrome' due to the characteristic deep bruising that appears hours after death. Street enforcers who carry it are considered especially cruel, as the weapon's delayed effect means victims often don't know they've been hit. Corporate wetwork teams prize it precisely because autopsies frequently misattribute cause of death to natural cardiovascular failure. Ownership is a marker of either serious institutional backing or dangerous black-market connections.

story_hooks: A string of deaths ruled cardiac arrest are revealed to share the PHE-3's wound signature — someone is running a quiet purge, and the only lead is a black-market parts supplier in the Fen District.

A player character is hit by a PHE-3 pulse during a firefight and doesn't realize it until they collapse twenty minutes later — they have hours to find treatment before internal hemorrhage becomes fatal.
An Arcturus Defense Solutions whistleblower claims the PHE-3's targeting algorithm was calibrated using non-consenting human subjects from a Lazarus Pharmaceuticals clinical program.
A stolen shipment of PHE-3 units surfaces in the hands of a radical anti-corporate cell — they're planning something public, something that will look like a mass medical event.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, angular carbine with a distinctly medical aesthetic corrupted by weaponization. The frame tapers from a bulbous emitter head down to a narrow stock, resembling a stylized syringe or surgical tool repurposed for lethality. Its silhouette is deliberately narrow and non-threatening at casual glance—a weapon designed to not *look* like one until the moment of discharge.
physical_description.dimensions: 68 cm overall length. Emitter head measures 12 cm in diameter with a recessed lens crown. Stock is 8 cm wide at grip. Depth profile averages 4 cm except at the photovoltaic capacitor housing (6 cm bulge mid-frame).
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively light at 3.1 kg—feels almost fragile in hand despite lethal purpose. Weight concentrates in the mid-body capacitor cluster, creating a forward-heavy balance that rewards braced shooting. Feels more like precision instrumentation than a combat weapon.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade titanium-aluminum composite frame with carbon-fiber grip panels. Emitter lens housing is reinforced borosilicate glass with ceramic heat-dissipation fins.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal gray with an iridescent oil-slick sheen across the capacitor housing—visible only under direct light, suggesting the photovoltaic charge state. Lens crown has a faint amber tint from NIR filtering coatings.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary. Accent colors: deep amber/orange lens ring, pale ceramic white heat fins, black rubberized grip.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured black polymer grip with shallow diamond knurling—designed for gloved hands. Cool to the touch due to passive heat-sink integration. Ergonomically contoured but deliberately minimalist, offering no comfort, only control.
distinctive_features: Recessed emitter lens with concentric amber-tinted focusing rings visible beneath borosilicate dome
Three stacked ceramic heat-dissipation fins running along starboard side, creating a surgical/medical instrument aesthetic
Dual photovoltaic capacitor cells visible as bulging housings on either side of the mid-frame, with subtle status LEDs (amber for charging, pale green for ready)
Absence of any visible barrel or muzzle—the weapon is all lens and housing
Fine engraved charging time readout (1.4s) etched into the stock in minimalist sans-serif font
Faint microcircuit traces visible beneath translucent panel sections on the left side of the frame
Cable routing channels for optional targeting optics along the dorsal surface
Deliberately exposed internal geometry—nothing is hidden, yet the weapon's true function remains obscure to untrained observers
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Ironside Armaments circular logo (a gear bisected by a rifle sight) stamped in relief on the left capacitor housing. Serial plate mounted on the stock (brushed steel, approximately 3×1.5 cm). Arcturus Defense Solutions microlicense marking etched below the emitter on the frame—small, easily missed.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field units show thermal stress patterns on the ceramic fins—faint browning or blotching from repeated firing cycles. Lens occasionally develops micro-fractures from shock. Grip panels wear smooth with use. Well-maintained examples retain the iridescent capacitor sheen; neglected units develop a dull, oxidized appearance. Combat-worn examples show scuffing on the composite frame and occasional scorching around the emitter housing from proximity discharge.
